material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Under the nominal 0.03 L aqueous/0.018 L organic contact, extractant X2 should give the largest single-contact target recovery into organic (~0.531) while retaining useful target/impurity selectivity (~4.69). X0 may purify more gently but sacrifices recovery. This assumes dossier indexing is reliable.

## H2 [tentative]
Reaction outcome likely depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and continuously on temperature/time; anonymous indices imply no ordering. Initial batches will screen catalyst/solvent combinations at matched charge and then vary severity around the best observed condition.

## Decision rule
Final recommendation must have assay purity at least 0.80; among eligible completed batches choose the highest measured recovery, treating small differences within assay uncertainty as unresolved and preferring a simpler/lower-risk process. A contrary extraction observation or repeated reaction result will revise these expectations.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [partly supported, scoped]
The dossier prediction that X2 can raise organic-phase purity is consistent with several final assays, but absolute recovery is strongly conditioned by upstream reaction and washing. Its indexing has not been contradicted; no direct extractant comparison has yet been made.

## H2 [supported only within the screen]
At 350 K/1800 s with 0.018 mol each reactant and 0.005 mol catalyst, catalyst C3 outperformed C0/C1/C2 in the S0 screen on reaction-mixture HPLC purity/recovery (events runner-operation-0006, -0026, -0043, -0060), though the first C0 batch is confounded by delayed component addition and a second heat. With C3, solvent S1 gave the highest observed pre-extraction recovery (0.130; event -0077); S2 was next (0.091; -0094), while S3 was poor (-0110). This is a categorical result, not an index trend.

## H3 [supported, process scope]
A 0.01 L wash after X2 extraction appears to impose substantial target loss: washed S1/C3 batch recovered only 0.020 in the final assay (-0087), whereas the unwashed S2/C3 batch recovered 0.039 (-0103) despite a lower pre-extraction recovery. This comparison is confounded by solvent; nevertheless, washing is suspended unless needed to cross purity 0.80. Testable consequence: unwashed S1/C3 should retain purity >=0.80 and improve recovery over -0087.

## Next decisions
Use unwashed C3/S1 as the working process and vary reaction temperature/time. If purity falls below 0.80, compare a smaller wash or more selective extractant; if recovery does not improve materially, investigate extraction volume/contact rather than assuming reaction optimization transfers downstream.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
The nominal X2 selectivity prior remained qualitatively useful. Increasing organic/aqueous contact ratio while keeping X2 changed downstream recovery substantially without destroying enrichment, although the exact dossier anchors did not predict the whole process.

## H2 [supported in tested C3/S1 scope]
For C3/S1 at 1800 s, raising temperature from 330 to 410 K increased pre-extraction HPLC recovery from 0.096 (-0126) through 0.171 at 370 K (-0142), 0.205 at 390 K (-0158), to 0.253 at 410 K (-0174). Because batches were not replicated, this monotonic numerical trend is evidence within this screen, not a precision kinetic law. At 420 K with a slightly larger charge, pre-extraction recovery was 0.279 (-0188), so the plateau/optimum remains unresolved.

## H3 [supported for process decision]
Omitting wash and increasing X2 contact from 0.018 L against about 0.080 L aqueous to 0.045 L against about 0.055 L gave the decisive downstream improvement: the 410 K batch achieved final recovery 0.143 at purity 0.811 (-0181). The 420 K/high-organic-ratio batch raised recovery to 0.172 but measured purity 0.798 (-0195), below the prespecified 0.80 constraint. This narrow miss is not treated as eligible despite assay uncertainty because selection is constrained by the observed threshold.

## Final decision
Recommend completed batch 11 (event -0181): C3/S1, 410 K for 1800 s, quench, 0.005 L aqueous plus 0.045 L X2, 240 s mix/120 s settle, retain organic, no wash/dry/concentration. It has the highest observed recovery among batches whose final measured purity is at least 0.80. This decision would change if repeat assays established batch 12 purity >=0.80 or if a replicated neighboring condition improved recovery while remaining clearly above the purity boundary.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–liquid-extraction–finishing system. The reaction generates a target reporter, impurities/byproducts, and possibly degradation material. Liquid–liquid partitioning then enriches the target in a selected organic phase. Washing, drying, concentration, sampling, and phase selection can change recovery even when they improve—or appear to improve—purity. The instrument outputs are synthetic reporter quantities, so this account concerns anonymous benchmark roles rather than real molecular identities.

### 1. Reaction stage

The important manipulated reaction variables were catalyst identity, solvent identity, temperature, duration, charge, and catalyst loading. Except for the first batch, the main screen used 0.018 mol each of limiting reagent and component, 0.050 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 1800 s heating, and 700 rpm stirring. Batch 12 used 0.020 mol of each reactant. Catalyst and solvent indices are categorical, not ordered physical descriptors.

A useful conceptual scheme is

reactants → target,
reactants → impurity/byproduct,
target or intermediates → degradation products.

For condition vector x, one could write effective rates

r_target = k_target(catalyst, solvent, T)·g(concentrations),
r_side = k_side(catalyst, solvent, T)·h(concentrations),

with Arrhenius-like temperature dependence as a plausible hypothesis, not an identified law. The data determine only net reporter outcomes after 1800 s; they do not separately determine rate constants, orders, equilibria, or degradation pathways.

#### Catalyst evidence

The cleanest catalyst comparison used solvent S0 at 350 K:

- Batch 2, C1: pre-extraction HPLC conversion 0.0938, purity 0.5435, recovery 0.00922, selectivity 0.497.
- Batch 3, C2: conversion 0.1258, purity 0.2525, recovery 0.0352, selectivity 0.242.
- Batch 4, C3: conversion 0.0986, purity 0.6027, recovery 0.0630, selectivity 0.572.

C3 therefore produced the best target recovery and purity of these three under the tested S0 condition, despite not giving the largest reported conversion. This shows that conversion alone is not a sufficient reaction objective: C2 converted somewhat more material than C3 but directed substantially less toward the desired reporter.

Batch 1 cannot provide a fair C0 comparison. It initially lacked the component when its HPLC measurement was made, then received 0.040 mol component and a second 1800 s heat. It also used 0.040 mol reagent and only 0.003 mol C0. Its final purity was 0.717 and recovery only 0.00077, but the altered sequence, charge, catalyst loading, and doubled heating confound catalyst identity.

#### Solvent evidence

With C3 at 350 K, the pre-extraction HPLC results were:

- Batch 4, S0: purity 0.6027 and recovery 0.0630.
- Batch 5, S1: purity 0.6174 and recovery 0.1302.
- Batch 6, S2: purity 0.6391 and recovery 0.0915.
- Batch 7, S3: purity 0.3262 and recovery 0.0489.

S1 gave the largest target recovery, S2 gave slightly higher measured purity, and S3 was clearly unfavorable in this screen. Because there were no replicates, these are condition-specific numerical rankings rather than precise estimates of categorical effects.

#### Temperature evidence

For C3/S1 and 1800 s, increasing temperature produced a monotonic rise in pre-extraction HPLC recovery over the directly comparable 0.018 mol charge series:

- Batch 8, 330 K: conversion 0.1281, purity 0.6143, recovery 0.0961, byproduct signal 0.0469.
- Batch 5, 350 K: conversion 0.2332, purity 0.6174, recovery 0.1302, byproduct signal 0.0647.
- Batch 9, 370 K: conversion 0.2863, purity 0.6482, recovery 0.1707, byproduct signal 0.0958.
- Batch 10, 390 K: conversion 0.3548, purity 0.6490, recovery 0.2052, byproduct signal 0.0986.
- Batch 11, 410 K: conversion 0.4031, purity 0.6544, recovery 0.2531, byproduct signal 0.1452.

A crude endpoint slope for recovery from 330 to 410 K is about (0.2531−0.0961)/80 ≈ 0.00196 K⁻¹, but the intermediate values are not exactly linear and no uncertainty-controlled replicates were performed. I therefore regard monotonic improvement over this screened interval as supported, while any linear or Arrhenius equation remains conjectural. Byproduct signal also generally rose with temperature, indicating a severity trade-off, although measured reaction purity stayed near 0.61–0.65.

Batch 12 at 420 K used the larger 0.020 mol paired charge, so it is not a strict continuation of that temperature series. It gave conversion 0.4200, purity 0.6612, recovery 0.2787, and byproduct signal 0.1334. It is consistent with continued improvement or an emerging plateau, but charge and temperature effects are inseparable.

### 2. Extraction stage

The nominal dossier supplied distribution coefficients for X2 of K_product = 2.585 and K_impurity = 0.552, with K_product/K_impurity ≈ 4.69. The campaign results are consistent with this dossier being qualitatively useful.

For one equilibrium contact, a simple partition model gives the fraction of species j transferred to organic phase as

f_j = K_j V_org / (V_aq + K_j V_org).

This model explains both recovery and enrichment trends surprisingly well, provided the reaction solvent is counted with the eventual aqueous-phase volume after `add_phase`.

For the standard extraction in batches such as batch 6, V_aq was approximately 0.050 L reaction solvent + 0.030 L added aqueous phase = 0.080 L, and V_org was 0.018 L X2. The dossier predicts

f_product ≈ 2.585·0.018/(0.080 + 2.585·0.018) ≈ 0.368,
f_impurity ≈ 0.552·0.018/(0.080 + 0.552·0.018) ≈ 0.111.

Thus target is extracted about 3.3 times more efficiently than impurity in terms of transferred fractions. Batch 6 entered extraction with HPLC purity 0.639 and recovery 0.0915; its final assay gave purity 0.8688 and recovery 0.0391. Multiplying 0.0915 by the predicted target fraction gives about 0.0337, close in scale to the observed recovery. Transforming the feed target/impurity odds by the predicted extraction enrichment gives a final purity near 0.86, also close to observation. This agreement supports an equilibrium-like partition mechanism, although other unreported solutes and instrument noise prevent exact closure.

Batch 11 deliberately changed the phase ratio to about V_aq = 0.055 L and V_org = 0.045 L. The model predicts f_product ≈ 0.679 and f_impurity ≈ 0.311. Starting from HPLC purity 0.654, the corresponding target/impurity enrichment predicts an organic purity of roughly 0.80–0.81. The final assay observed purity 0.8110 and recovery 0.1429. The predicted target recovery from the HPLC value alone is 0.2531·0.679 ≈ 0.172, somewhat above the observed 0.143, plausibly because of handling losses, sampling, incomplete equilibration, additional impurities, or differences between HPLC and final-assay estimands.

Batch 12 used approximately V_aq = 0.052 L and V_org = 0.048 L. The same model predicts f_product ≈ 0.705 and f_impurity ≈ 0.337. Its feed purity of 0.661 would imply final purity around 0.80, consistent with the measured 0.7985. Its measured final recovery was 0.1716, versus a simple prediction of about 0.2787·0.705 ≈ 0.196. Thus the phase-ratio model correctly anticipated the direction and approximate magnitude of the recovery/purity trade-off, but it is not an exact mass-balance model.

The other extractants were not experimentally compared, so their dossier indices remain unvalidated. X2 cannot be claimed globally optimal; it is merely the only extractant tested and behaved consistently with its favorable nominal K_product and selectivity.

### 3. Washing and finishing losses

A 0.010 L wash appears costly in target recovery. Batch 5 entered extraction with recovery 0.1302. With the standard X2 phase ratio, the partition model would place roughly 0.048 of the original charge in organic phase, yet the washed final product recovered only 0.0201 at purity 0.8616. Batch 6 omitted washing and recovered 0.0391 at purity 0.8688, despite having a lower pre-extraction recovery of 0.0915. This comparison is confounded by S1 versus S2, but the direction and magnitude strongly suggest wash-mediated target loss without a necessary purity benefit in this range.

Batches 2–5 included a 0.010 L wash, drying, and 300 s concentration. Their final recoveries were only 0.0143, 0.0130, 0.0147, and 0.0201. Batches 6–10 omitted the wash but retained drying/concentration; their final recoveries included 0.0391 at 350 K, 0.0504 at 370 K, and 0.0547 at 390 K for favorable C3 conditions. Batch 11 omitted washing, drying, and concentration altogether and retained the selected organic phase directly, reaching 0.1429 recovery. Batch 12 used the same simplified finish and reached 0.1716 recovery. Phase-ratio changes and reaction severity are major co-changes, so the independent effects of drying and concentration are unidentifiable, but no evidence showed that they were needed for purity.

A plausible process equation is

R_final ≈ R_reaction · f_product(K_product,V_org,V_aq) · η_handling,

where η_handling combines incomplete separation, wash loss, sampling, drying/concentration loss, and mismatches between analytical estimands. For batches 11 and 12, comparison with the dossier partition prediction gives rough η_handling values of about 0.83 and 0.87. These are descriptive derived values, not universal constants.

Final purity can be approximated from feed target/impurity odds:

odds_final ≈ odds_feed · f_product/f_impurity,
purity_final ≈ odds_final/(1 + odds_final),

with deviations expected from byproducts not represented by the two-species calculation.

### 4. Interpreting the final-assay conversion values

Most final assays reported conversion near 0.99–1.00, even where the pre-extraction HPLC conversion was only 0.09–0.42. For example, batch 11 had pre-extraction HPLC conversion 0.403 but final-assay conversion 0.983; batch 12 had 0.420 versus 0.999. I do not interpret that discrepancy as evidence that extraction chemically converted nearly all remaining reactant. The public contract explicitly warns that reaction and downstream metrics follow their own instrument contracts and are not necessarily assays of the same material. Phase selection can also remove reactant from the analyzed sample. Therefore, pre-extraction HPLC values are the better basis for relative reaction-condition comparisons, while final purity and recovery are the appropriate downstream decision metrics.

### 5. Why batch 11 was recommended

The operating objective required measured final purity of at least 0.80 and then favored recovery. Batch 11—C3/S1, 0.018 mol of each reactant, 0.005 mol catalyst, 410 K for 1800 s, quench, 0.005 L aqueous phase, 0.045 L X2, 240 s mixing at 700 rpm, 120 s settling, organic-phase selection, and no wash/dry/concentration—gave final purity 0.8110 and recovery 0.1429. It had the highest observed recovery among batches meeting the stated purity threshold.

Batch 12 produced higher recovery, 0.1716, but measured purity was 0.7985 and therefore failed the literal ≥0.80 requirement. Its miss is small relative to typical assay noise scales, so scientifically its eligibility is uncertain near the boundary; operationally, however, it was correctly treated as ineligible based on the observed value rather than retroactively relaxing the constraint.

### 6. Scope and unresolved alternatives

The conclusions apply only to the tested anonymous materials, charges, 1800 s reaction duration, single-stage extraction, and chosen agitation/settling conditions. Important unidentifiable or weakly identified factors include:

- Reaction order, activation energies, equilibrium limits, and separate formation/degradation rate constants.
- Whether temperature or the larger charge caused batch 12’s improvement.
- Effects of catalyst loading, reaction duration, solvent volume, stirring speed, pressure, atmosphere, and reactant ratio; these were not independently varied.
- True repeatability: every principal condition was run once, so process variability and categorical effects are partly confounded.
- Independent effects of washing, drying, and concentration, because these operations changed alongside solvent, temperature, or phase ratio.
- Extraction kinetics versus equilibrium. Contacts used 240 s mixing and 120 s settling; no contact-time series was performed.
- Whether X0, X1, or X3 could outperform X2 at an optimized phase ratio or in multistage extraction.
- The contribution of byproducts beyond the single nominal impurity in the two-species partition calculation.
- The exact relationship among HPLC recovery, HPLC yield, final-assay yield, and final-assay conversion.

Plausible alternative explanations are that the apparent temperature trend partly reflects batch variability; that changing phase ratio altered phase behavior or analytical sampling rather than only equilibrium partitioning; or that omitted finishing operations avoided losses unrelated to the nominal target distribution coefficient. Nevertheless, the combined consistency of the temperature series and the quantitative phase-ratio calculation makes a coupled reaction-selectivity plus equilibrium-partition model the most economical explanation of the observed campaign.

payload.rationale: I treated the aqueous inventory at extraction as the 0.028 L reaction solvent plus 0.012 L added phase. For X2 I used the dossier partition coefficients (Ktarget≈2.585, Kimpurity≈0.552) with f=KVorganic/(Vaqueous+KVorganic), and applied the same relation again to aqueous washing. This predicts the paired directions: longer heating raises upstream recovery (Q02>Q01); X0 gives higher purity but much lower recovery than X2 (Q03 versus Q04); less organic extractant raises purity and lowers recovery (Q05 versus Q06); washing raises purity while losing target (Q08 versus Q07); two staged washes slightly outperform one equal-volume wash in purity with a small recovery penalty (Q10 versus Q09); and concentration gives a small purity gain with modest loss (Q12 versus Q11). Upstream predictions are substantially extrapolated because these recipes use C1/S2, omit the added component, use only 0.00025 mol catalyst, and include charges and reaction times outside the directly comparable campaign series. The low-charge recipes have much more catalyst per mole of reagent and were therefore assigned much higher fractional upstream recovery than the 0.04 mol recipes. Intervals are deliberately broad to include uncertainty in that catalyst/charge scaling, unmeasured time dependence, wash and finishing losses, the HPLC sampling step, and final-assay variability.

payload.report:
1. **Supported, contradicted, and untested claims.** An instance prior was supplied, but only for extraction: the nominal dossier gave distribution coefficients for X0–X3. No reaction-rate law, catalyst ranking, solvent ranking, or complete-process optimum was supplied. The X2 partition claim was qualitatively supported: a simple equilibrium calculation described the purity and recovery scale of batches 6, 11, and 12 reasonably well. However, the claim that X2 is the best extractant remains untested because only X2 was used experimentally. The self-developed claim that C3 was preferable under the S0 screen was supported by batches 2–4: batch 4 had higher pre-extraction recovery and purity than batches 2 and 3. C0 was not fairly tested because batch 1 had delayed component addition, a different charge and catalyst loading, and two heating periods. The solvent ranking S1>S2>S0>S3 for recovery under C3 at 350 K was supported numerically by batches 4–7, but without replication. The monotonic temperature–recovery relationship was supported from 330 to 410 K by batches 8, 5, 9, 10, and 11; a linear or Arrhenius law was not established. Batch 12 did not cleanly extend that series because its charge changed. The proposed wash-loss effect was supported only suggestively: washed batch 5 recovered 0.0201, whereas unwashed batch 6 recovered 0.0391 despite lower pre-extraction recovery, but solvent identity also changed. The judgment changed most after batch 6 showed that washing was not required for high purity, after batches 9–11 established the temperature trend, and after batch 11 showed that a larger X2 phase ratio could raise recovery to 0.1429 while retaining purity 0.8110. Batch 12 then established the practical boundary: recovery rose to 0.1716, but measured purity fell to 0.7985, contradicting any assumption that maximizing organic fraction would preserve eligibility indefinitely.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would run one C3/S1 reaction at the batch-11 condition, homogenize the quenched feed, and split it into matched aliquots. One aliquot would receive the standard low-organic extraction ratio and the other the batch-11 high-organic ratio. I would assay the common feed and both organic and aqueous phases, without washing, drying, or concentration. The equilibrium-partition explanation predicts both phase recoveries from the same X2 coefficients and predicts approximate closure of organic plus aqueous target mass. Agreement across both ratios would strengthen the distribution-law explanation and isolate phase ratio from reaction variability. If the phase ratio changed purity as predicted but total target mass failed to close, I would instead assign substantial loss to phase handling or sampling. If apparent distribution depended strongly on ratio or failed in both phases despite mass closure, I would favor nonideal partitioning, incomplete equilibration, or additional solute interactions. If the standard and high-organic aliquots gave nearly identical recoveries, the batch-11 improvement would more likely have arisen from batch-to-batch reaction variation rather than extraction geometry.

3. **Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects.** Raw characterization spectra were not analyzed; only processed estimates were used. GC, IR, MS, NMR, and UV–visible measurements were unused. No replicate condition was run, and atmosphere, pressure, catalyst loading, solvent volume, reaction duration, stirring, settling time, and reactant ratio were not independently identified. X0, X1, and X3 dossier values were unused experimentally. Final-assay conversion values near unity were not used as reaction evidence because they disagreed strongly with pre-extraction HPLC conversion and referred to a different selected material. Native score was also not used to override the stated purity/recovery objective.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q02 and especially Q07–Q12: they extrapolate to C1/S2, omit the added component, use a much smaller absolute catalyst charge, extend reaction time, and—particularly for Q07–Q12—use a 0.002 mol reagent charge with a catalyst-to-reagent ratio far outside the campaign. Predictions comparing X0 with X2 are also uncertain because X0 was never tested. Relative paired directions, such as washing lowering recovery or more organic phase increasing recovery, are more reliable than their absolute point estimates. The batch-11 recommendation is the best literal observed choice, but its robustness is limited because purity 0.8110 was close to the 0.80 boundary and no replicate was obtained; batch 12’s 0.7985 result shows that assay or process variation could reverse the ranking near that boundary.

The assigned goal materially affected evidence collection. Because every completed batch required a final assay and the goal prioritized recovery subject to purity ≥0.80, the campaign shifted rapidly from catalyst/solvent screening to exploitation of C3/S1/X2 and phase-ratio optimization. That improved the final operating recommendation but left fewer opportunities for replication, extractant comparison, kinetic identification, and matched wash or finishing controls. This is a design trade-off rather than clear evidence that the recommendation is wrong.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 11 had the highest observed final recovery among completed batches meeting the required measured purity threshold: recovery 0.1429 and purity 0.8110. It used catalyst C3/solvent S1 at 410 K for 1800 s, then a high X2 organic-to-aqueous contact ratio and retained the organic phase without washing. Batch 12 recovered more (0.1716) but its measured purity was 0.7985, below 0.80, so it was not eligible.
